blocks.html: Sorting means arranging data in a particular order:

items.html: Ascending order: smallest to largest (1, 5, 9) or A to Z.
Descending order: largest to smallest (9, 5, 1) or Z to A.
The merit list of the Bihar Board results, sorted by marks in descending order.
Contacts on your phone, sorted alphabetically.
Online shopping: "Sort by price: low to high".
A cricket points table, sorted by points and then by net run rate.
Attendance registers, sorted by roll number.
Faster searching. Binary search (Chapter 6) works only on sorted data and is much faster than checking every item.
Easy reading. People find information quickly in an ordered list.
Finding the smallest, largest and median values becomes easy.
Finding duplicates. In a sorted list, equal values sit next to each other.

blocks.html: In this chapter we sort arrays of integers in ascending order. To sort in descending order, only the comparison sign changes (> becomes < ).

Idea: Compare each pair of neighbouring elements and swap them if they are in the wrong order. After the first pass, the largest element has "bubbled up" to the last position, just as an air bubble rises to the top of water. Each later pass places the next largest element, so every pass has one less element to check.

items.html: Repeat for pass = 1 to n − 1:
For j = 0 to n − pass − 1: if arr[j] > arr[j+1] , swap them.
If no swap happened in this pass, the array is already sorted, so stop early.

items.html: The swapped flag is the optimisation. Without it, the outer loop always runs n − 1 times, even for an array that is already sorted.
For descending order, change arr[j] > arr[j + 1] to arr[j] < arr[j + 1] .

blocks.html: Idea: Divide the array into a sorted part (on the left, empty at the start) and an unsorted part. In each pass, select the smallest element from the unsorted part and swap it with the first element of the unsorted part. The sorted part grows by one element each pass.

Think of a teacher arranging students by height: she looks along the whole line, picks the shortest student and sends them to the first place, then picks the shortest of the rest for the second place, and so on.

items.html: Repeat for i = 0 to n − 2:
Assume min = i .
For j = i + 1 to n − 1: if arr[j] < arr[min] , set min = j .
If min != i , swap arr[i] and arr[min] .

blocks.html: The bold part is sorted. After n − 1 = 4 passes, the last element is automatically in its correct place.

items.html: Selection sort makes at most n − 1 swaps, fewer than bubble sort. This helps when swapping is costly, for example when moving large records.
It always makes n(n − 1)/2 comparisons, even when the array is already sorted. It cannot stop early.

blocks.html: Idea: This is how most people arrange playing cards in their hand. Pick up the next card and insert it into its correct place among the cards already arranged. Larger cards slide one place to the right to make room.

items.html: Repeat for i = 1 to n − 1:
key = arr[i] (the card being inserted).
j = i - 1 . While j >= 0 and arr[j] > key : shift arr[j] one place right

blocks.html: (arr[j+1] = arr[j] ) and decrease j .

items.html: Put the key in the gap: arr[j+1] = key .

blocks.html: The bold part is always sorted, and it grows by one element each pass.

items.html: If the array is already sorted, the while loop never runs, and insertion sort finishes after only n − 1 comparisons. This makes it the best of the three for nearly sorted data.
It shifts elements instead of swapping them, which costs fewer assignments.
It works well when data arrives one item at a time, such as adding a new score to a sorted leaderboard.

lessons.title: 5.5 How fast is a sort? Time complexity

blocks.html: The speed of a sorting method is measured by how the number of steps (mainly comparisons) grows as the number of elements n grows. This is called time complexity, and it is written in Big-O notation.
In the worst case, bubble sort compares (n − 1) pairs in pass 1, (n − 2) in pass 2, and so on down to 1. The total is:
For n = 5 this gives 5 × 4 / 2 = 10 comparisons. The term n²/2 grows fastest, so we say the sort takes O(n²) time ("order n squared"). If the data doubles, the time becomes about four times longer.

items.html: Sorting arranges data in ascending or descending order. It makes searching, reading and analysis easier.
Bubble sort compares and swaps neighbouring elements. After each pass, the largest remaining element is in its final place. A swapped flag lets it stop early.
Selection sort finds the smallest element of the unsorted part and swaps it to the front. It always makes n(n − 1)/2 comparisons but at most n − 1 swaps.
Insertion sort takes each element and inserts it into the sorted part by shifting larger elements right. It is very fast for nearly sorted data.
All three are O(n²) in the average and worst cases. Bubble sort (with the flag) and insertion sort are O(n) in the best case.
A stable sort keeps equal items in their original order. Bubble and insertion sort are stable, and selection sort is not.
std::sort (<algorithm> ) is O(n log n). Use greater<int>() for descending order
